(A Guideline for Section Heads) 


—by Liz Greenway 
Camp Oconto 


When people ask “just what do you do all day?” it’s 
rather hard to explain. You know that you’re busy but 
you’re certainly not doing the kinds of things for which 
hero cookies are awarded. In fact, being a section head is a 
humbling kind of experience, or should be, since you know 
you're doing a good job when no one notices that you’ve 
taken your half day or 48 hours off or even been out on a 
short canoe trip. The section should just hum along without 
you. 

Don’t misunderstand me: you can’t just sit back and 
expect a well run section to happen. You are a supervisor, 
a co-ordinator and a positive force towards creating that 
well-run section. Where other counsellors teach activities 
and deal with tangibles, you are expected to keep tabs on 
the feelings or the mood of the section - very much an 
intangible. So the initial question should read, “just what 
do you try to do all day?” 

The job of supervision is a delicate one. The process 
involves constant evaluation, feedback, awareness and com¬ 
munication with the counsellors. It is they who deal most 
directly with the campers and it is the section head’s job to 
help the counsellor explore the most effective means of 
approaching her campers. The section head attempts to help 
the counsellor think for herself, arriving at her own decision 
or approach. 

One of the most important aspects of this evaluation and 
one that often gets overlooked, is praise. As a section head, 
you are constantly trying to make the section run better or 
more smoothly. This, however, does not mean always cor¬ 
recting what is wrong but also acknowledging what is right. 
This section that you work with is made up of people and 
praise, even for small progress, is essential for all of us. It’s 
rewarding to be noticed when we try to do something well. 
If the praise is honest it also increases the chances of some¬ 
one making an honest attempt to repeat the effort. 

At the same time it seems that most problems arrive at 
your doorstep. You are a sounding board or an open ear for 
people with problems, people who just want to talk or 
people who don’t know what they want — both campers 
and counsellors. It’s hard, but necessary, to remember the 
truism that bad advice is worse that no advice. We shouldn’t 
always try to solve someone’s problems for them since 
learning to cope with your own problems is part of growing 
up. Perhaps it is wise not to get too hung up on solving the 
world’s problems all at once but simply provide that 
friendly open ear. 

Many problems that counsellors come to you with are, 
in fact, no longer problems. They may already know the 
approach to take but they want a chance to say it out loud 
and receive your moral support. You provide confidence 
more often than you provide ‘wonder-cure’ solutions. This 


means understanding the needs of that particular counsellor 
and where you can best support her. 

Although problems often are real enough to the people 
involved, you have to keep things in perspective, to keep a 
sense of humour (you’d better believe it!) and to put the 
focus on the positive solution. This doesn’t mean to ignore 
the problem, but there’s no point in dwelling on things too 
long: move out and move on or you’ll all be frustrated. 

People tend to develop a lot of problems when they get 
over-tired or later in the evening when things have quieted 
down and they have time to think. Before leaping to astute 
psychological analyses cope with the minor problems first: 
things like fatigue, a particularly hot, humid day, loneliness 
due to no mail (male?!), misunderstanding or lack of com¬ 
munication. 

Once a problem has been recognized, however, there is 
no point in fuddling about with it. Do something. Take time 
to think, since people deserve more than a flippant approach, 
ask for help if you need it from the assistant director but 
then do something positive to correct the situation.

secretary and his leadership in the Executive Development Workshop;

One of the major problems that a section head deals with is that of discipline - 
campers and counsellors. . . That sense of perspective and the positive approach 
will prove invaluable. 

To help avoid most counsellor problems, I found it best to make a specific 
effort to speak to each counsellor alone every week or so, to talk over any prob¬ 
lems and to get some feedback. You don’t need to tell the counsellor that she’s 
scheduled for an interview since that can sound rather formidable but you should 
make an interview schedule for yourself. It’s awfully easy for the time to slip by. 
Suddenly it’s the third week of camp and you haven’t had a chance to sit down 
and talk for twenty minutes without being interrupted. This is in addition to your 
regular staff or section meetings. 

Finally there comes the part that I enjoy most. You can avoid most camper 
problems through awareness or what I call ‘cruising’. It’s beneficial particularly in 
the first two weeks of camp to walk through the section near or at the beginning 
of each of the periods. You may find someone alone in the tent and it’s a good 
chance to stick your head in the tent to talk to her. Everyone doesn’t have to be 
doing something all the time, since it is the summer vacation, but if it’s the same 
girl three periods in a row then perhaps there is some problem. She may need some 
friendly interest (which is not the same thing as prying) or a little encouragement. 
At any rate you need to be aware of what is, or is not, going on in the section, so 
that corrective action can be taken. 

When you do take a day off, appoint one of your counsellors to be responsible 
for the section. They’ll appreciate the responsibility and maybe they’ll even 
understand your job a little better. However, when you get back don’t ask them 
what they did all day. You’ll probably get thrown in the lake! 

So that’s the section head’s job as I see it. You have to listen, be aware, be 
available, be honest, be positive and keep tabs on the section by accepting feed¬ 
back from your staff and campers. That’s not too much eh!
